cover.headline: A real CDMO transformation, priced as if it were already finished: Laurus's own history supports ~38.5x earnings; the price pays ~66x
cover.lead: Laurus Labs makes anti-retroviral (ARV) medicines and their ingredients for about a third of the world's HIV patients and has become one of India's larger contract manufacturers (CDMO) for drug innovators. Of FY26 revenue of ₹6,813 cr, 28% was CDMO for innovators, 3% Laurus Bio (fermentation), 40% generic APIs and 29% formulations. Q1FY27 was a record: revenue +29% to ₹2,026 cr, CDMO +69% to ₹835 cr, EBITDA margin 31.5%. The stock nearly doubled from ~₹1,009 at end-March to ₹1,980 on 30-Sep-2026, above 7 of the 9 post-results targets and level with or below the other 2 (median ₹1,820). Brokers that disclose a method mostly use **P/E** (Motilal Oswal 65x 12-month forward, BOBCAPS 55x Jun-28E). Our EPS of ₹24.6 / ₹27.6 / ₹32.1 for FY27-29E is in line with the street. Laurus's own one-year-forward P/E median since 2021 on EPS before exceptional items (35.6x, trough years left out) times the pharma sector factor (×1.082) gives **38.5x Sep-28E EPS of ₹29.8 = {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with SELL**. Cross-checks: EV/EBITDA ₹1,194, DCF ₹458. Bull case {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear case {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.p: CDMO rose from ~14% of revenue in FY20 to 31% in FY26 and 43% in Q1FY27 (with Bio). Three patented APIs went commercial in 18 months, 55% of CDMO revenue is now commercial supply, a new big-pharma client joined in Q1, and capex is tied to named customer demand. The USFDA record is clean (21 inspections, no active warning letter). We do not dispute the quality of the turnaround.

arguments.h: It is still lumpy and capital-hungry
arguments.p: Laurus has done this before: one large order lifted CDMO to ₹2,167 cr in FY23 and its end cut it to ₹922 cr in FY24, taking EPS from ₹14.7 to ₹3.0. Today 45% of CDMO revenue is Phase III and launch supply. Capex doubles to ₹2,000 cr in FY27 (~24% of sales), asset turns are ~0.9x and free cash flow turns negative in FY27E on our numbers.

We model CDMO +58% in FY27 and +20% a year after, an EBITDA margin of 30.0-31.0% (management: ">30%") and EPS growing ~24.9% a year to FY29E. Our FY27E/FY28E EPS (₹24.6 / ₹27.6) sits beside the street average of the brokers we could read (₹24.4 / ₹28.4).

At ₹1,980 Laurus trades at 66.4x our Sep-28E and 71.8x FY28E EPS, almost double its 35.6x five-year median. Our 38.5x target multiple already includes the FY22 boom years and a sector premium. Even our bull case ({{scen.bull.tp|inr}}) sits below today's price. The rule would turn us buyers below ~₹1,000.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): whether CDMO revenue holds near the Q1 run-rate of ₹835 cr (management: "plus/minus ₹100 crores") and the margin stays near 30%.
Conversion of Phase III CDMO programmes to commercial supply; validation of the commercial peptide block (from Q2FY27) and any disclosed peptide contract.
Commissioning milestones: Laurus Bio's 400 KL fermentation plant (by Dec-2026), the first Unit 7 block (commercial validation by Mar-2027), the KRKA JV formulation plant (Phase I mid-2027).
ARV: tender pricing, donor funding and the uptake of long-acting injectables, where Laurus has no lenacapavir licence.
Capex and debt: FY28 capex guidance and the start of the 532-acre Laurus Pharma Zone (>USD600 mn over ~8 years).

sections.title: Two businesses on one chemistry platform: contract manufacturing for innovators, and low-cost generic medicines led by anti-retrovirals

blocks.p: Laurus makes active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs, the chemical in a medicine that does the work), intermediates and finished tablets. It reports two divisions. **CDMO** (contract development and manufacturing) makes patented molecules to an innovator's process, from clinical batches to commercial supply, for human health, animal health and crop science, plus fermentation products through Laurus Bio. **Affordable Medicines** (its name for generics) sells generic APIs and its own formulations, led by anti-retrovirals (ARVs) for HIV, where Laurus supplies about a third of the world's patients through global-health tenders, plus oncology, cardiovascular, diabetes and gastro products and long-term contract supply of generics (CMO). It runs 15 manufacturing sites, mostly around Visakhapatnam, with ~8,800 KL of reactors, 12 bn tablets a year of formulation capacity and ~8,126 employees (FY26). About 67% of FY26 revenue was exported; no customer was over 10% of revenue (AR FY26).

blocks.p: **What Laurus means by CDMO.** All CDMO revenue is innovator work on patented molecules; contract manufacturing of off-patent products is booked as CMO inside Affordable Medicines (Head CDMO, 24-Jul-2026). Most clinical programmes are APIs or advanced intermediates rather than early starting materials, which ties Laurus to a customer for the life of the molecule. Management names no customer, molecule or contract value, and will not give segment margins.

blocks.callout: **So what:** Laurus is a generic-medicines company that has used its chemistry, scale and regulatory record to build a contract-manufacturing business now worth ~₹2,100 cr of revenue and rising fast. The ARV franchise is the cash engine; CDMO is the growth engine; Bio and advanced biologics are options. Investors are paying for the second and the third, but cannot see the economics of any single contract.

sections.title: Twenty-one years: an ARV specialist, one boom, one bust, and a founder who kept investing through both

blocks.p: Dr. Satyanarayana Chava founded Laurus in 2005 as a research-driven API maker and built it around anti-retrovirals, where low cost and backward integration win tenders. It listed in December 2016. The founder still runs the company as CEO, with his son Krishna Chaitanya Chava heading CDMO, his daughter Soumya Chava heading generics and commercial, and V. V. Ravi Kumar CFO since 2006 (AR FY26). The numbers fall into four eras.

blocks.callout: **Lesson from history:** the FY23 order shows how a single CDMO contract can add ~₹1,200 cr of revenue and disappear within a year. The CFO says FY23 was "the best year because of that execution of large purchase order" and that the team then "had not so great results" for seven quarters (24-Jul-2026). Management argues today's CDMO revenue is spread across many products with no concentration; it is far broader than in FY23, but it is not yet proven through a full cycle.

sections.title: Industry: outsourcing and China+1 favour Indian CDMOs; the ARV market is mature, donor-funded and facing long-acting injectables

blocks.p: **Contract manufacturing is the growth engine.** Laurus cites a global small-molecule CDMO market of ~USD 85 bn (2025) growing over 7% a year to 2034, and an Indian market of ~USD 2 bn growing over 14% (Sep-2026 presentation). HDFC Securities expects the Indian contract research, development and manufacturing (CRDMO) market to reach ~USD 15 bn by 2029 (13.4% a year), India's share of the global market to rise from 3.8% to 4.7%, and manufacturing outsourcing by innovators to rise from 24% (2024) to 39% (2029). The drivers: price pressure on innovators (US drug-pricing laws), the China+1 strategy and the US BIOSECURE Act, more complex molecules, and new peptide capacity needs.

blocks.p: **ARVs are a mature, tender market.** Laurus serves about one-third of the global HIV population. Its ARV revenue has been ₹2,500-2,800 cr for five years and management expects it to stay around ₹2,800 cr, with pricing "broadly constant" in FY26. The company describes a stable market funded by multilateral agencies, steady dolutegravir use and adoption hurdles for long-acting injectables. The risk is longer-term: Gilead licensed its twice-yearly injectable lenacapavir to six generic makers for 120 countries in Oct-2024, and Laurus is not one of them. **Costs:** the West Asia war raised solvent prices from late February 2026; Laurus reported "some impact" in Q4FY26 and "some pressure" in Q1FY27, without supply disruption.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the tailwinds that matter most for the next three years (outsourcing and China+1) reach Laurus directly, and the numbers show it. The ones that excite the market most (peptides, biologics) are real capabilities but not yet revenue, and the ARV franchise that funds it all faces a slow structural threat from long-acting injectables.

sections.title: CDMO: broader and more commercial than in the FY23 boom, but 45% of today's revenue is still launch and Phase III supply

blocks.p: Small-molecule CDMO revenue was ₹384 cr in FY20 and ₹917 cr in FY22, spiked to ₹2,167 cr in FY23 on one very large purchase order, fell to ₹922 cr in FY24 when it ended, and has rebuilt to ₹1,374 cr (FY25) and ₹1,896 cr (FY26, +38%). Q1FY27 was ₹835 cr (+69%), a run-rate of ~₹3,300 cr a year. What has changed since FY23: (1) three patented APIs went commercial in the 18 months to Apr-2026, early in their patent lives, with multi-year customer forecasts and no destocking seen; (2) 55% of Q1 CDMO revenue was commercial supply (50% in FY26), most of the rest Phase III supply, and one customer's product has just won global approval; (3) management says no customer, product or therapy area is a concentration risk, and that "molecules generating ₹200 crores or more" exist; (4) the active pipeline grew from ~90 projects (FY23) to >125 across human health, animal health and crop science; (5) a new big-pharma client was added in Q1FY27.

blocks.p: Laurus names no customers and gives no contract values, citing confidentiality; the CEO dismisses project counts because "one program may give $500,000, one program may give $50 million". What it does say: customers want validation at commercial scale on the same equipment train before they award a product, so Laurus builds capacity first (the reason FY24 hurt); the FY27-28 capex is "for a purpose, for a product and capacity" needed by existing partners, across multiple customers and products, mostly APIs rather than intermediates. Animal-health APIs are already shipping commercially (Laurus Synthesis, ₹491 cr turnover in FY26); crop science needs "a couple of more financial years". Peptides: a commercial-scale block is being validated from Q2FY27, with GLP-1 and other programmes, but no project details. Customer advances were ₹645 cr at Mar-2026 (₹395 cr a year earlier); none were received in Q1FY27.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** this is a far better CDMO business than the one that collapsed in FY24: more products, more commercial supply and visible customer demand behind the capex. But Q1's ₹835 cr includes launch and Phase III stocking that can pause, and management itself calls the business "lumpy, but predictable". We model ~₹720 cr a quarter for the rest of FY27 (CDMO +58% for the year) and +20% a year in FY28-29E as Unit 7 and the peptide block fill.

sections.title: Affordable Medicines: an ARV cash engine with flat volumes, and a non-ARV formulation business that is growing

blocks.p: Affordable Medicines (generic APIs and formulations) grew 18% in FY26 to ₹4,733 cr and 10% in Q1FY27 (API +3%, formulations +22%). ARVs are about 60% of it: ₹2,807 cr in FY26, two-thirds API and one-third own formulations, and ₹669 cr in Q1FY27 (API ₹415 cr, formulations ₹254 cr). Management says FY26 ARV sales beat its usual "₹2,500 crores plus or minus ₹200 crores" because ARV assets were fully used, that ARV pricing was broadly constant, and that ARV revenue will stay around ₹2,800 cr while its share falls. Growth comes from non-ARV products: oncology, cardiovascular, diabetes and gastro APIs, developed-market launches (6 approvals in FY26; 96 dossiers filed) and integrated contract supply (CMO) for generic partners, helped by 20% more tablet capacity in FY26.

blocks.p: **The ARV risk is slow, not sudden.** Laurus serves about a third of the world's HIV patients, mostly through donor-funded tenders. The company describes a stable market with "adequate funding by multi-lateral agencies" and steady dolutegravir use, and says long-acting injectables face adherence and retention challenges. But Gilead's royalty-free licences for twice-yearly lenacapavir went to six other generic makers (Oct-2024). If long-acting regimens take share in prevention and later treatment, Laurus's ARV volumes would shrink without a licence of its own. Emerging-market registrations and a new South Africa office (Q1FY27) widen the non-ARV base.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** a solid, cash-generating generic business whose ARV half will not grow and whose non-ARV half grows in the low teens. We model generic API +4% / +5% / +5% and formulations +12% / +10% / +10% (FY27-29E), taking Affordable Medicines to ₹5,841 cr by FY29E. The KRKA JV's formulation plant (Laurus 49%) is equity-accounted and adds no revenue.

sections.kicker: Segment: Bio, cell and gene therapy
sections.title: Laurus Bio and the cell and gene therapy bets: real capabilities, ~3% of revenue, and returns that management itself puts four to five years out

blocks.p: **Laurus Bio** (78.34% owned; formerly Richcore Lifesciences, bought in January 2021 when its revenue was ~₹50 cr) makes products by precision fermentation: enzymes for biocatalysis, animal-origin-free cell-culture ingredients, and contract fermentation of food proteins, colours and polymers. FY26 revenue was ₹184 cr (+15%; standalone turnover ₹200 cr, profit ₹6.7 cr) and Q1FY27 ₹35 cr (+21%). Its four 45,000-litre fermenters in Bangalore are fully used; a 400 KL plant at Vizag (initially industrial chemicals, surfactants and polymers moving from Bangalore) is due by Dec-2026, with room for 600 KL more. The CEO says the next 12-18 months decide "which molecule, which program in our precision fermentation will take off", and that Bio and crop science together (~₹250 cr revenue) need 18-24 months to assess. An outside investor holds the 21.66% minority (a ~₹120 cr strategic private-equity investment, per HDFC Securities; non-controlling interest ₹131 cr in the balance sheet).

**Advanced biologics.** (1) **Cell therapy:** a 34.89% stake in ImmunoACT (equity-accounted; ₹126 cr invested), whose CAR-T therapy NexCAR19 reached >660 infusions by Jun-2026; a second plant (+2,500 treatments a year) opened in Mar-2026 and Cipla is partnering it in South Africa. (2) **Gene therapy and ADCs:** a process-development lab opened in Dec-2025 and a >65,000 sq ft cGMP site in Hyderabad (investment >₹200 cr) is due for qualification by mid/end-2027. (3) **Aarvik:** Laurus invested USD2 mn in Aarvik Therapeutics and in-licensed two pre-clinical ADC assets for India (Jul-2026), which need GLP toxicology and Phase I-II trials over 3-4 years. These push R&D to 5.8% of sales in Q1FY27 (₹118 cr, incl. ₹35 cr capitalised).

sections.title: Capacity: ₹4,256 cr of capex in five years left asset turns below 1x; the next ₹3,500 cr is backed by customers, management says

blocks.p: Laurus spent ₹4,256 cr on capex in FY22-26 (cash flow basis) against ₹4,797 cr of operating cash flow, so free cash flow over the five years was close to nil. Gross block rose from ₹3,028 cr (Mar-21) to ₹6,943 cr (Mar-26) and reactor volume to ~8,800 KL. Revenue per rupee of gross block fell from 1.6x (FY21) to 1.0x (FY26); the CFO puts the asset turn at 0.89x and management targets "a little over 1.0" in the medium term. Capex now steps up again: ₹1,070 cr in FY26 (15.7% of sales), ₹394 cr in Q1FY27, ₹2,000 cr guided for FY27 (twice raised from ₹1,000 cr) and ">₹3,000 crores" over FY27-28, "we may do more". Beyond that sits the 532-acre Laurus Pharma Zone at Vizag, a >USD600 mn, ~8-year plan starting from end-FY27.

sections.title: Competitive advantage: a real cost and scale moat in ARVs, a credible but young one in CDMO, and no pricing power

blocks.p: A moat is a lasting advantage that lets a company earn more than its cost of capital for longer than rivals. Laurus has one in ARVs, where scale and backward integration make it the lowest-cost supplier for a third of the world's HIV patients, and a younger one in CDMO, built on chemistry, fungible large-scale capacity and a clean regulatory record. Neither gives pricing power: ARV tenders and generic APIs are won on price, and CDMO customers can and do dual-source. Returns show it: ROE ranged from 4% to 45% in five years, and core return on capital was below the cost of capital in FY24-25.

blocks.callout: **Verdict:** a genuine but narrow moat. Process chemistry, scale and regulatory reliability are hard to copy and explain why innovators keep adding projects; switching costs last only for the life of each molecule; ARVs and generic APIs have no pricing power; the new modalities are capabilities, not yet advantages. Divi's, Sai Life, Neuland, Syngene, Piramal Pharma and Chinese CDMOs compete for the same work. We would pay for the franchise, but not for a moat it has not yet proved through a cycle.

sections.title: Quality and USFDA status: a clean record across 21 USFDA inspections, no active warning letter or import alert, and no recalls in five years

blocks.p: For a contract manufacturer the regulatory record is the licence to operate: innovators will not file a supplier that might draw a warning letter. Laurus's record is strong. Since inception its sites have had 21 USFDA inspections and 115 inspections by all regulators (WHO-Geneva, ANVISA, PMDA, European agencies), with establishment inspection reports (EIRs, the USFDA's closing document) at all key sites; CARE found no active USFDA warning letter or import alert at company-owned facilities as of June 2026. It reports zero product recalls in the last five years, 132 customer and regulatory audits in FY26 and 24 in Q1FY27 without critical findings. Seven of its fifteen sites are USFDA-approved. The one serious incident in our review was a December 2022 fire at a Vizag unit, after which process safety was upgraded; there were no reportable incidents in FY25-26 (CARE).

sections.title: No seasonality to speak of, but lumpy: CDMO deliveries and ARV tenders move quarters, and the margin has climbed for nine quarters

blocks.p: Laurus has no true seasonality. Quarters move with CDMO shipment timing (customers order campaigns, not monthly volumes) and with ARV tender deliveries, which pushed formulations to ₹607 cr in Q3FY26 and back to ₹451 cr in Q4. The trend matters more than the pattern: the EBITDA margin rose from ~14% in Q1FY25 to 31.5% in Q1FY27 as CDMO revenue rose from ₹214 cr to ₹835 cr a quarter, gross margin climbed from 55% to 62.7% and fixed costs were spread over more revenue.

sections.title: Four acts: an ARV ingredient maker to FY20, a three-year boom, a one-year bust, and a CDMO-led rebuild that has now passed the old peak

blocks.p: Laurus grew revenue from ₹1,327 cr in FY15 to ₹2,832 cr in FY20 (~16% a year) as an anti-retroviral (ARV) ingredient maker earning 15-21% EBITDA margins. FY21 changed everything: revenue jumped 70% to ₹4,814 cr on an ARV formulation and API surge, the margin hit 32% and EPS rose from ₹4.8 to ₹18.3. FY22-23 held revenue up, FY23 helped by one very large contract-manufacturing order, but ARV prices were already falling. When that order ended in FY24, revenue fell 17%, the margin collapsed to 15.5% and EPS to ₹3.0, with new plants adding cost before revenue. The rebuild since has been led by contract manufacturing for innovators (CDMO): revenue +10% in FY25 and +23% in FY26 to ₹6,813 cr, margin 26.2%, EPS ₹16.5. Q1FY27 EPS of ₹6.8 takes trailing EPS to ~₹20, above the FY21 peak for the first time.

blocks.p: Laurus's EBITDA margin (before other income) was 20% in FY20, 32% in the FY21 boom, 26-29% in FY22-23, 15.5% in the FY24 trough and 26.2% in FY26; Q1FY27 reached 31.5%. Two things drive it. **Gross margin** (revenue less materials) moved from ~52% (FY24) to 60.4% (FY26) and 62.7% (Q1FY27) on a richer CDMO mix, softer raw-material prices and process improvements (CFO, 30-Apr-2026). **Operating leverage**: employee and other costs are largely fixed, so they fell from 36% of revenue in FY24 to ~31% in Q1FY27 as revenue grew; the CEO says commercial CDMO supply earns more than development work at a similar gross margin because fewer scientists are needed. Against that, R&D rose to 5.8% of revenue in Q1FY27 (gene therapy and ADC build-out), solvent costs rose with the West Asia war, and each new plant adds people and overheads before it earns.

blocks.p: Laurus has funded its growth with debt and reinvestment, not equity. Net debt was ₹2,285 cr at Mar-2026 (1.25x EBITDA) and ₹2,656 cr at Jun-2026 (1.28x) as capex picked up. Free cash flow (operating cash flow less capex) was close to zero in every year from FY21 to FY25 and only turned clearly positive in FY26 (₹554 cr), helped by higher profit and customer advances (₹645 cr at Mar-2026 vs ₹395 cr a year earlier). Working capital is heavy: inventory ~317 days of material cost and receivables ~115 days (Screener), a cash conversion cycle of ~263 days. CARE (3-Jul-2026) rates the bank debt AA (Stable) and calls liquidity strong, with ~60% use of ₹2,000 cr of working-capital lines.

sections.title: Capital allocation: reinvest almost everything, borrow the rest, pay a token dividend; returns are back above the cost of capital, but only just in core terms

blocks.p: Laurus has put nearly all its operating cash into plants for five years. In FY22-26 it generated ₹4,797 cr of operating cash flow, spent ₹4,256 cr on capex, ₹779 cr on interest, ₹408 cr on dividends and ₹284 cr on stakes in associates and the JV (ImmunoACT, KRKA, Ethan Energy, Kurnool Renewables), and borrowed a net ₹920 cr. It has made one acquisition of note (Richcore, ₹245 cr in FY21) and issues shares only for ESOPs. The dividend is ₹2 a share (12% of FY26 EPS; yield ~0.1%). ROE recovered from 4% (FY24) to 18% (FY26) and return on operating capital (excluding cash) to ~18%. We forecast ROE of {{F.roe.0|pct}} / {{F.roe.1|pct}} / {{F.roe.2|pct}}: above the ~12.3% cost of capital, below the 45% of FY21.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a better business than the market paid ₹300 for in 2023, but not one worth twice its history

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** an ARV leader that supplies a third of the world's HIV patients at low cost, turned into one of India's larger contract manufacturers for innovators: CDMO 43% of Q1FY27 revenue, three patented APIs in commercial supply, >125 projects, a clean USFDA record and capex tied to customer demand, plus options in fermentation, peptides, cell and gene therapy and ADCs. Earnings should grow ~24.9% a year to FY29E on our numbers.

**What you are paying:** 66.4x our Sep-28E and 71.8x FY28E EPS after the stock doubled in six months. Our 38.5x Sep-28E multiple is Laurus's own 2021-26 median (35.6x, trough years out) lifted 8.2% for a sector trading above its history, and gives {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}). The EV/EBITDA cross-check agrees (₹1,194); the DCF (₹458) says cash flows support far less. The price assumes the CDMO ramp continues for years without a stumble.

blocks.p: **Is it a SELL on the business?** No. We expect strong earnings growth and our forecasts sit with the street. The stock is a SELL because the rule compares the price with a target built from the multiple the market has paid for Laurus over five years, and the price (~66.4x Sep-28E EPS) is far above it, above even our bull case. Momentum, index inclusion and a strong Q2 could keep the stock high for a while; we would revisit the multiple only on public evidence of a structurally larger CDMO business (disclosed commercial contracts, sustained commercial share above 60%, asset turns back above 1.2x), not on price.
